Tech Report: Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1417 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious.
  • But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared remains the subject of intense debate.
  • According to recent reports, this is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men.".

But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared remains the subject of intense debate.

According to recent reports, this is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust. Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history.

In a recent development, "I do think this is nonsense," notes Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposedly be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case.".

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story.

The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers. The juxtaposition highlights the contrast between colonial violence and the industrialized mass murder of the Holocaust. Yet it also points to connections: Whips were used in Nazi concentration camps, while Fascist Italy deployed chemical weapons against civilians and soldiers during its invasion of Ethiopia (then Abyssinia) in 1935-36.

In the 1930s, anti-colonial thinkers from India to the Caribbean argued that colonialism and fascism were two sides of the same coin. "There is nothing newly introduced or original about the blustering exploits of Hitler and Mussolini," observed the Trinidadian journalist and Pan-Africanist George Padmore in 1938. "They have all been used before by the British in their efforts to obtain the subjection of less powerfully armed and more industrially backward people.".

European colonial rule was marked by the ruthless exploitation of people and resources, often enforced through extreme violence. In "The Origins of Totalitarianism" (1951), German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt argued that colonial territories served as laboratories for racial ideologies and practices of domination that could be applied beyond the legal constraints of Europe. Arendt described how these later "boomeranged" back into Europe and helped shape totalitarian politics in distinct and unprecedented form.

The Congo Free State, King Leopold II of Belgium's private colony from 1885 to 1908, became notorious for its extreme brutality, as colonial authorities used executions, amputations and sexual violence to ensure rubber production quotas were met. Forced labor was also central to Nazi rule, with millions of Poles, Ukrainians, Russians and others from the Soviet Union, and Jews, subjected to exploitation and "Vernichtung durch Arbeit" ("extermination through work"). Within a few years, the regime mobilized around 13 to 14 million forced laborers, a scale comparable to the transatlantic slave trade over more than three centuries. The Nazis sought to extract value from their victims at every stage, confiscating their property, exploiting their labor, and even harvesting gold teeth and hair from the dead.

In a recent development, while racism underpinned both colonial empires and Nazism, Malinowski says the goals were different. The colonial powers tended to present assimilation as a path to advancement, forcing colonized people to adopt European culture, serve imperial interests, and suggesting that a select, educated few could gain opportunities at elite institutions such as Oxford or Cambridge. "This is definitely not something that the Nazi regime is offering to Poles or to Russians or let alone to Jews," added Malinowski.

"In terms of violence, colonial violence was just as extreme as Nazi violence. But Nazi violence was annihilatory and exterminatory compared to colonial violence in the colonies," indicates Edward Kissi, a historian at the School of Interdisciplinary Global Studies at the University of South Florida. He points to the example of how, unlike European colonial powers in Africa, the Nazis pursued the elimination of Black-Germans or peoples of African descent in Germany through forced sterilization. "Even in racism, colonial color-based racism and colonial anti-Jewish sentiments were fundamentally different from what the Nazis pursued.".

Industry observers note that on October 2, 1904, German General Lothar von Trotha issued the "Vernichtungsbefehl" ("extermination order") following the Herero uprising in German South West Africa (present-day Namibia). Historians generally attribute the order to a combination of racial ideology, a desire to terrorize the population into submission, and efforts to secure colonial control over land, labor and resources. Between 1904 and 1908, an estimated 60,000 to 80,000 Herero (around 80% of the population) and 10,000 (around half the population) Nama died.

One area where the exhibition draws no direct parallel is the industrialized killing carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau. "Where the two things really diverge is the Holocaust and is the systematic mass murder of the European Jews and it's murder for the very purpose of murder," explains Malinowski. The deportation of around 1,800 Jews from the Greek islands of Rhodes and Kos in July 1944 illustrates how Nazi persecution often defied military or economic logic. Even after the war was effectively lost, the community was transported to Auschwitz, where most were murdered immediately upon arrival.

The issue of the "singularity" of the Holocaust came to the fore during the 1980s "Historikerstreit" ("historians' dispute"). Historian Ernst Nolte argued that Nazism should be understood in the wider context of 20th-century political violence, and as a response to Bolshevik terror in particular. Critics accused him of downplaying German responsibility for Nazi crimes.

Since 2020, a renewed debate dubbed the "Historikerstreit 2.0" has focused on whether the Holocaust should be viewed as a unique reference point in German memory culture or be understood alongside the histories of colonialism, racism and empire. The dispute now is less about the legitimacy of comparison than about its implications.

It has been revealed that the mass murder of tens of thousands of the Herero and Nama during four years of German colonial rule is now regarded as the first genocide of the 20th-century. In 2016, Nama representatives walked out of talks after Germany's chief negotiator said what happened was "incomparable" to the Holocaust. The German government has since recognized the events as genocide "from today's perspective," but it has not yet accepted legal liability or agreed to pay formal reparations.

Martinican intellectual Aime Cesaire argued in "Discourse on Colonialism" (1950) that Europe condemned under Nazism forms of violence it had long accepted in its colonies. The exhibition opens amid renewed debates over settler colonialism, the definition of genocide, and the meaning of "never again," sharpened by Nicaragua's case against Germany at the International Court of Justice over German support for Israel during the war in Gaza. These tensions are reflected in visitors' comments in the exhibition's epilogue, even though the exhibition itself does not address Israel or Palestine beyond a reference to Mohammed Amin al-Husseini, appointed Grand Mufti of Jerusalem in 1921.

Sources indicate that germany has unequivocally accepted responsibility for the Holocaust, which is front and center of the country's culture of remembrance. However, Kissi likens Germany's apparent reluctance to reckon with its colonial history to debates in the US over slavery, in Cambodia over the Khmer Rouge, and in Turkey over the Armenian genocide. According to him, Germany's contemporary identity cannot be fully understood without examining its colonial history and the ways the Nazis appropriated and transformed aspects of that legacy. "I think Germans and all other human beings who have experienced violent pasts and difficult pasts should be very careful not to delink or dissociate those facts from their present," Kissi said. "These are historical patterns. It is better to deal with these historical patterns and discomforts than to just fight them and then say this has absolutely nothing to do with German national identity.".

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence" is on show at the German Historical Museum until April 11, 2027.

It's not quite a five-year mission, but as Star Trek celebrated its 60th anniversary in September of this year (we may have mentioned it once or twice), I decided it was high time I finally watched the original Star Trek.

Sources indicate that before this year, I hadn't seen a single episode of "Star Trek: The Original Series", as it's now known. I'm a millennial; I grew up on "The Next Generation", "Deep Space Nine" and "Voyager". By comparison, the old series (TOS) always looked so… old and naff whenever I saw clips of it.

Sources indicate that but now I have seen the original series. Over the course of 2026, I've ploughed through all 79 episodes, spread across three seasons. And you know what? It's pretty damn good. Even with the shiny 2006 remasters, you'll have to prepare yourself for some bad special effects work, but the scripts are interesting, the sci-fi concepts are out there, and the acting — especially from Shatner and Nimoy — is top-notch.

And just as I finally discovered a love for this classic sci-fi series, what should drop into my lap? Why it's the latest Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge diorama set from Lego. Now I have more on my wishlist to add to the Best lego space sets.

Industry observers note that let's start with the Band-Aid rip: this set is $200. I know; it stings, especially when Star Trek promised us a future where money doesn't exist. But at 1701 pieces (nice, I see what you did there), it's much better value from a bricks-per-dollar perspective than the X-Files set we checked out recently.

Still, that's no small investment for a toy, even if it will make a lovely display piece when it's built.

Industry observers note that as the name suggests, you get a full Lego-ified recreation of the bridge of the USS Enterprise (NCC-1701, no A, B, C, or D). This includes Captain Kirk's chair, the helm positions ahead of him (manned by Chekov and Sulu), and all of the surrounding computer displays where you usually find Spock, Uhura and Scotty.

There's even a viewscreen that can sit in front of the crew, displaying an adorable Klingon commander facing off against Kirk.

Industry observers note that board the legendary starship and meet the crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 for an amazing building experience. Recreate the iconic bridge and transporter room that served as the backdrop for epic scenes from "Star Trek: The Original Series".

It has been revealed that alongside the main bridge, there are a few fun extras bolted on, including a rotating transporter pad (which can make minifigures "disappear") and a working turbolift door connected to the back of the main bridge diorama. You'll have to make the swoosh sound effect yourself, though.

It's a wonderfully faithful recreation of Kirk's command center, complete with computer panels and screens, swiveling chairs and that weird scope thing that Spock was always looking into.

That remarked, it's a little lacking in proper Easter eggs. There are some tribbles hiding around the build, and the monitors have custom stickers showing cool Trekkie things. The weapon display racks on the back hold an array of pointy Klingon blades, Starfleet phasers, Sulu's fencing rapier and even Spock's harp, but compared to, say, the X-Files set we built recently, it feels a bit lacking in those deep-cut references.

In a recent development, all in all, it's a fantastic little diorama, but when it was revealed, I'll admit I was a little puzzled as to who it was aimed at. "Star Trek fans, duh!" is the obvious response, but the Venn diagram crossover between "people who are nostalgic for the original series of Star Trek" and "people who want to buy $200 Lego sets" has to be pretty small, right?

Star Trek first aired way back in 1966, which means the first generation of fans are now 70 years old and upwards. Lord knows I hope I'm still building Lego sets when I'm 70, but is that a large enough crowd to make this set a success? Then again the show was repeated and syndicated throughout the 70s and 80s, which means hopefully there'll be some younger buyers, too.

Recent findings suggest that the playset aspects of the set are even more puzzling. The working door, exploding monitor and spinning transporter pad are great additions to a kids' playset, but this isn't that — it's a display for nostalgic Star Trek fans. The design of the set just feels a bit confused.

According to recent reports, but then it hit me. Maybe this isn't just for fans of the original series; maybe it's meant to create some newly introduced fans. I started watching the original Star Trek 60 years after its debut because… well, I'm the sci-fi editor for a space website, and it felt wrong that I hadn't seen it. But most people don't have that sort of professional impetus. The average person won't jump back to watch a 60-year-old TV show without a polite nudge, and this set does a great job of highlighting the charm and optimism of Star Trek's debut outing.

Recent findings suggest that I don't know, maybe I'm just projecting here. Maybe Lego bought the rights to make Star Trek sets and needed something to do after they'd mined all the nostalgia they could from the excellent Enterprise D set they released in 2025. Maybe this is just a toy for major kids.

Or maybe… just maybe, it's meant to inspire the next generation of Star Trek fans to check out where the magic started.

Industry observers note that disclaimer: We were sent a copy of the Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge set by Lego.

But Therabody, the innovative tech giant behind Theragun, offers more than relief for sore muscles and pain. It now sells a broad repertoire of wellness gadgets aimed at alleviating ailments like eye strain, menstrual cramps, and skin puffiness (to name a few). So whether you’re shopping for a fitness lover or someone who could use a little self-care, there’s likely a Therabody gadget worth wrapping up.

Sources indicate that updated November 2026: I’ve added the Theragun Prime (6th Gen) and removed discontinued products. I also confirmed up-to-date links and prices.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

If you’re looking for a professional-grade massage device, the Theragun Pro Plus is one of the most advanced percussive guns on the market, incorporating vibrations, heat, and near-infrared LED therapies for an all-in-one recovery tool. It also offers cold therapy, but you'll have to purchase an additional attachment for $100 to make use of that capability—a steep add-on for what is already a splurge. After testing the attachment myself, I don't think it justifies the cost unless you are sure you'd regularly use the contrast therapy.

According to recent reports, priced at $650, this is the most expensive Theragun, so I'd recommend it to athletes or those who are dealing with chronic muscle pain and want the LED therapy. For casual people, some of the features might feel like overkill. For example, there's a built-in biometric sensor for heart rate tracking that I have barely used. I do, though, appreciate the OLED screen, which displays a force meter, so you can see exactly how much pressure you're applying. It's a useful function if you need a nudge to apply more pressure or a reminder to ease up.

The Theragun Prime (6th Gen) hits the sweet spot between the elite Pro Plus and the budget-friendly Relief. It’s still a premium percussive massage gun, with five speed settings, two attachments (a dampener and standard ball), and up to 120 minutes of battery life. You won’t get extras like heated or near-infrared LED therapy, or compatibility with Therabody’s cold and vibration attachments, but you will enjoy top-notch durability. It’s the only Theragun in the lineup rated to withstand drops from up to 10 feet, making it an excellent gift for the accident-prone person in your life.

The Theragun Relief, introduced in 2023, remains the cheapest Theragun—priced even lower than the Mini Plus. For the price tag, you’re sacrificing some of the premium features, like the LCD screen and Bluetooth connectivity to the Therabody app for device control. But you can still follow guided routines on the app, and the simple one-button control is refreshingly simple to use.

It has been revealed that the Relief comes with three head attachments and has three speed settings, which is a step down from models that offer a standard five speeds and four or more attachments. Still, the Relief is less than half the weight of the Pro Plus, and it's equipped with the essentials, which is more than enough for the average person.

Recent findings suggest that the original Theragun Mini is still a solid portable device—and it's $60 less—but the Mini Plus feels like a shrunken version of the elite Pro Plus. The ergonomic triangular design lets me target trigger points and muscle groups like my hamstrings and calves with more pressure control (though, admittedly, that same shape makes it awkward to use on my lower back). Thoughtful details, like a travel lock to prevent it from powering on and a compact carrying pouch, make it easy to carry on commutes and flights.

Most notably, it brings heated percussive therapy to a travel-friendly device. The heat therapy is easily my favorite feature on the Pro Plus. The Mini Plus is also compatible with Therabody's Vibration Plus and Cold Plus attachments (both sold separately).

Note: Some customers have reported charging issues, saying their units wouldn't power up, but I haven't run into any battery problems in my two weeks of testing. I'll revision this review if anything shifts with long-term use.

Sources indicate that the JetBoots Pro Plus are full-length, wireless boots that combine pneumatic compression with vibration therapy and infrared LED light. Everything is controlled from a built-in LCD screen and control panel on the lead boot, and connectivity is effortless, automatically linking when powered on.

It has been revealed that eight preset programs target legs, knees, and joints, but you can manually adjust pressure, intensity, and the session length. Sessions can run from 10 to 60 minutes in five-minute increments, with compression adjustable between 20 and 100 millimeters of mercury (mmHg)—a standard unit of measurement for pressure. Vibration offers three intensity levels (low, medium, and high), and the infrared LED setting is a simple on or off, with an automatic shutoff after 45 minutes.

It has been revealed that inside the boots, a nonporous proprietary material reduces moisture and microbial buildup, and after months of testing, I haven't noticed any lingering odors. These are best suited for athletes, frequent travelers, or anyone managing circulation-related conditions. Conveniently for those aforementioned jet-setters, the JetBoots Pro Plus are TSA-approved for carry-on travel; just keep in mind that they're pretty hefty.

According to recent reports, I enjoyed the original TheraFace Mask, but the upgraded TheraFace Mask Glo feels like the smarter purchase. It's easier to find (Therabody seems to be phasing out the original), costs $270 less, and is slightly lighter at 1.13 pounds versus the OG's 1.27 pounds. While the Glo has fewer LED bulbs—504 compared to 648—the difference doesn't translate to a lesser treatment. You get the same red, infrared, and blue light wavelengths, plus the signature vibration therapy that made the first-generation mask stand out.

Industry observers note that the vibrations are now integrated into the adjustable straps rather than the mask itself. They're usually distracting, occasionally even headache-inducing, depending on my mood. I usually skip the vibration setting altogether to make this component less irritating. Even without it, the Glo remains competitively priced among high-end LED masks.

Industry observers note that treatment sessions range from four to 12 minutes, and the removable eye shields are thoughtful, but I prefer taking them off to extend the light coverage to my under-eye area. I very much appreciate the cordless design, but I do miss the display stand that came with the original. I often end up storing it back in its box, which makes me less inclined to reach for it. If you, too, deal with this matter, you might consider buying a travel case for $80.

Industry observers note that I challenge you to stay awake through a full session with the SmartGoggles 2.0. I’ve been testing them for months, and more often than not, I conk out while wearing them. The combination of gentle heat, vibration, and massage therapy across my forehead, eyebrows, and temples relaxes my facial tension within minutes. I love wearing them when I have a headache from staring at screens all day, and while I don’t struggle with regular migraines, I can see them being a soothing blackout remedy in a quiet, dark room.

Recent findings suggest that former reviewer Medea Giordano loved the first model, and this upgrade improves the fit with contoured padding that feels similar to Therabody’s SleepMask. You still get three preset modes: Focus, Sleep, and SmartRelax. That last option uses biometric feedback to adjust vibration patterns based on your heart rate. It also syncs with the Therabody app, letting you tweak the vibration and heat intensities or incorporate sound therapy. Note, though, if you’re a side-sleeper, you’ll have to shift around, as these are most comfortable while lying flat on your back.

I’ve tested several sleep masks, and the TheraFace SleepMask is among my favorites. Many claim to be 100 percent blackout, but this one leaves me feeling totally disoriented when I wake up, with no idea what dimension I'm in—just how I like it. The contoured padding feels plush, and the adjustable strap keeps the mask in place without tugging at my hair, even when I shift around at night. It comes with a carrying case, so I always pack it for travel.

It has been revealed that the selling point is that this mask uses vibrations—three pattern presets (Pulse, Wave, Constant)—designed to nudge your brain into deeper rest. I struggle with staying asleep, but when I wake up in the middle of the night, I just tap the button to start a 15-minute session, and it usually lulls me back to sleep. That stated, the vibrations are almost too gentle; you barely feel them, but you can absolutely hear them. It's not as soothing as a white noise machine, so if you're a light sleeper, this might be a deal-breaker.

The TheraFace Depuffing Wand has become a staple in my travel bag. It delivers both hot and cold therapy to help reduce puffiness, improve circulation, and enhance product absorption before completing your skin care routine. It’s TSA-friendly—zero awkward bag checks and counting—and ideal for tackling under-eye bags after a long flight or night. The curved applicator reaches every contour of my face, and the precision tip is great for trickier spots like under my eyes. The wand comes with three preset temperature levels that feel gentle but effective. While the cold function isn’t as icy as a roller fresh from the freezer, it’s consistent throughout a six-minute session and doesn’t drip. Plus, this one won’t crack if you forget to take it out of the freezer (RIP to two of my traditional rollers). An indicator light flashes at three minutes to remind you to switch sides, but this notification is easy to miss if you’re not looking straight into a mirror.

Cupping is an ancient healing technique that uses suction to provide muscle relief. Therabody's version combines suction, heat, and vibration therapy for localized recovery. With three levels of suction (30, 40, and 50 kilopascals, or kPa), three heat intensities (41, 43, and 45 degrees Celsius), and three vibration modes (low, high, and wave), I appreciate how you can customize the intensity of your session. The TheraCup is also programmed with an auto-shutoff after three minutes—so you don’t overdo any area—and built-in safety sensors that will cut off the pressure if it exceeds 60 kPa.

TheraFace Mask for $650: The TheraFace Mask is a cordless, hands-free light-therapy device that uses three wavelengths (red, infrared, and blue) to tackle different skin care goals. As a distinguishing feature from its competitors, the TheraFace Mask includes a built-in vibration therapy mode that massages pressure points around the eyes, brow line, and scalp for some added stress relief. Industry News: Dig review: Amy Poehler and Parks and Recs Mike Schur have done it again

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first time Amy Poehler and Mike Schur teamed up for a series about Poehler rolling up her sleeves and getting to work in a massive dirt pit, they gave us Parks and Recreation, a charming workplace sitcom about the power of friendship and doing what you love.
  • Story-wise, the two indicates are miles apart.
  • Kicking off that group is Elise (Poehler), the lead archaeologist on a long-running dig in southern Greece.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first time Amy Poehler and Mike Schur teamed up for a series about Poehler rolling up her sleeves and getting to work in a massive dirt pit, they gave us Parks and Recreation, a charming workplace sitcom about the power of friendship and doing what you love. The second time Amy Poehler and Mike Schur teamed up for a series about Poehler rolling up her sleeves and getting to work in a massive dirt pit, they gave us Peacock's new series Dig, which is — you guessed it! — a charming workplace sitcom about the power of friendship and doing what you love.

Story-wise, the two indicates are miles apart. Literally. The former takes place in the decidedly unglamorous town of Pawnee, Indiana, while the latter, based on Kate Myers' novel Excavations, transports us to a sun-bleached archaeological dig in Greece. Yet despite the flashy location and a new mystery twist, Dig retains the core formula that made Parks and Recreation so irresistible: investing deeply in a lovable new crew of unlikely friends.

Kicking off that group is Elise (Poehler), the lead archaeologist on a long-running dig in southern Greece. She's qualified and passionate, yet has a hard time connecting with the undergraduates (or UGs) participating in the dig. Because of her more guarded exterior, she's consistently second fiddle to longtime dig leader Neville (Hugh Laurie). Perpetually on the brink of retirement, Neville seems unable to cede control of the dig to Elise, both because of his love for archaeology and the ego boost his role gives him. He's the Lucy to Elise's Charlie Brown, constantly yanking the football away at the last second.

Industry observers note that so, when Elise discovers a perfectly preserved statue of Hera at an older dig site, the last thing she wants to do is tell Neville and give him an opportunity to claim any shred of credit. However, hiding any cultural artifacts from Neville and the Grecian government at large is illegal, so Elise must assemble a crack team to help her cover up her covert dig of the Hera statue, whom they nickname "Pretty Woman." First up is Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), an always flaky wild card who has unfinished business at the dig. Joining her are Clare (Antonia Thomas), a prim and proper conservator born with a silver spoon in her mouth, and Patty (Fina Strazza), a sheltered farm girl with a deep passion for Greek mythology.

Recent findings suggest that like with most sitcoms, the characters begin as the broadest versions of themselves before revealing their deeper nuances. At first, Elise is prickly to a fault, allowing Poehler to sidestep any preconceived comparisons you might want to draw to Leslie Knope. Elsewhere, Dylan is the hottest of hot messes, Clare is a haughty queen bee, and Patty is an out-of-her-depth klutz. They border on parodies instead of full-bodied characters, making Dig's earlier episodes a bit lukewarm.

It has been revealed that but as Dig's title suggests, this is a show that won't be satisfied by sticking at surface level. As the show delves into what makes its characters tick, it becomes a heartwarming tale of found family, not unlike many other beloved Schur shows. Suddenly, character traits that felt one-note to start are revealed to be defense mechanisms or misconceptions, adding entirely new dimensions to Dig's core four.

Dig works best when that core works together in earnest, which is another reason why the show's early entries feel like slower burns: They're doing the groundwork to loop every woman into the Pretty Woman dig. Once they're all on the same page, Dig gets off and running — even more so once Pretty Woman mysteriously vanishes, leaving Elise and her motley crew to do some boots-on-the-ground detective work. Thus begins a madcap caper involving stakeouts, undercover identities, and the black market.

Along the way, Elise, Dylan, Clare, and Patty are allowed to be wonderfully messy and vulnerable, all while staying refreshingly supportive of one another. For example, a love triangle burbles up between Clare, Dylan, and Clare's fiancé/Dylan's ex-boyfriend Gary (Jon Pointing), yet the storyline never devolves into cat fights or possessiveness. Instead, Dig focuses more on what these relationships mean to Clare and Dylan beyond romance. For Clare, her engagement is a sign of stability and true adulthood, whereas Dylan is looking for closure, something she notoriously can never get.

Industry observers note that dig also dabbles in intergenerational conflict, highlighting the differences between each of its leads, all of whom are at very different stages in their lives. Again, Dig doesn't take a hackneyed "Gen Z versus millennials versus Gen X" route. It's more interested in showing the different wants that motivate us. Patty yearns for belonging and friendship, while Elise wants to cement her legacy and make sure she's done something big enough to call her own, no Neville required.

Once Dig's ensemble truly comes together, they mesh wonderfully. Poehler brings a weary exasperation to Elise that slowly gives way to warm leadership, a transformation that's a joy to witness. Thomas and Viswanathan are perfect foils, the former a picture of poise, the latter completely uninhibited. Watching them feed off each other offers up a perfect comedic contrast. Finally, there's Strazza, whose endearingly goofy Patty becomes the beating heart of the show. Laurie, too, is a joy, blending Neville's smarminess with a genial charm that makes him infuriatingly tough to hate.

In focusing on archaeology, Dig emphasizes the importance of excavating ancient objects and interrogating the stories of those who once used them. In many ways, Dig is doing the same thing with its characters: peeling back their layers to get at their core truths. Only instead of using trowels and brushes, Dig uses the power of the workplace sitcom. It's a power Schur and his collaborators know well, and the result is a show that will leave you feeling like you've just uncovered something great in a dig of your own — with far less dirt on your face and clothes, that is.

#59339. Latest Update: Sleuth finds ‘impossible proteins’ in hundreds of research papers

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1222 w)

Latest Update: Sleuth finds ‘impossible proteins’ in hundreds of research papers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1222 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some studies show the expression of proteins such as caspase-3 (pictured), in cell lines that should not be able to produce them.
  • A scientific sleuth has identified more than 220 research papers that describe impossible patterns of protein expression in genetically altered cell lines.
  • Journals are now taking action to clean up the literature by retracting or correcting the work, and researchers warn that there are probably many more affected studies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some studies show the expression of proteins such as caspase-3 (pictured), in cell lines that should not be able to produce them. Credit: Dr Mark J. Winter/Science Photo Library.

A scientific sleuth has identified more than 220 research papers that describe impossible patterns of protein expression in genetically altered cell lines. In these studies, particular proteins show up in imaging experiments, even though the cells do not have the gene necessary to make them.

Journals are now taking action to clean up the literature by retracting or correcting the work, and researchers warn that there are probably many more affected studies.

According to recent reports, “This problem will not go away,” says Thierry Soussi, a cancer geneticist at Uppsala University in Sweden, who notes that there are several other examples of the issue in now-retracted papers that were not included in the sleuth’s analysis. “This is only the tip of a gigantic iceberg.”.

Cell lines are groups of cells derived from a single origin cell and cultured for use in experiments. Some cancer cell lines have been genetically modified with mutations and deletions — often to remove genes that usually control cell division. This means that the cultures continually divide and grow, giving researchers the chance to study tumour progression and test potential treatments.

Industry observers note that the MCF-7 cell line is one of these. It lacks the gene for caspase-3 protein, which is involved in cell death. In 2009, researchers warned1 that some studies that report working with MCF-7 have mysteriously observed caspase-3 expression in western blots, an imaging technique that identifies proteins based on their molecular weight.

Sleuth identifies dozens of studies that used the wrong antibody.

Sleuth identifies dozens of studies that used the wrong antibody.

In the most recent analysis, published as a preprint on 21 October to the data repository Zenodo2, Sholto David, a sleuth based in Arbroath, UK, finds that this problem persists and extends to other cell lines.

Industry observers note that david compiled a list of 20 commonly used cell lines with genetic mutations or deletions that leave cells unable to express specific proteins. He then scoured the literature using Google text and image searches to identify examples of western-blot images that unexpectedly identify these proteins. He also searched a collection of 140,000 articles that he had previously downloaded and screened for image-integrity complications and other problems, most of which were biomedicine papers.

He found 230 reports of phantom proteins across 221 papers published since 2004. The most common errors were observations of caspase-3 expression in the MCF-7 cell line, affecting 49 papers; expression of the cell-death protein BAX in the Jurkat cell line in 47 papers; and expression of the signalling protein STAT3 in the PC-3 cell line in 35 papers.

David suggests several explanations for these impossible protein-expression patterns. They might be the result of honest errors: researchers could have misidentified the cell lines or contaminated them with others. Or the antibodies used to identify proteins in the western-blot experiments could have been non-specific and bound to another protein with the same molecular weight. In fact, David claims that he stumbled across the anomalous proteins while working on a project that flagged hundreds of studies that used the wrong antibodies in experiments.

Another possibility is that some of the papers are the product of papermills, companies that fabricate and sell scientific manuscripts. David indicates that some papers in the cache contain the hallmarks of being produced by such outfits, including duplicated images or text templates that are similar to other papers. The proportion of the papers that fall into this category is not clear, he says.

Nature has contacted several authors of papers containing anomalies to ask for comment, but none responded.

Science sleuths raise concerns about scores of bioengineering papers.

Science sleuths raise concerns about scores of bioengineering papers.

Uri Ben-David, a cancer biologist at Tel Aviv University in Israel, states that David’s analysis confirms a problem that many researchers had suspected was an issue, owing to previously documented individual examples.

Industry observers note that “Conclusions built on these blots may be wrong, and other groups may have spent time and money building on them,” says Ben-David. “It is a reminder that a band on a western blot is not proof that a protein is there.”.

It has been revealed that another possible contributing factor is that cell lines are not genetically stable, he states. His previous work3 has shown that the same cell line grown in different laboratories can vary substantially. “Across 27 strains of MCF-7, we found extensive genetic diversity that affected gene expression and drug response. So the ‘MCF-7’ in a given lab is not necessarily identical to the reference MCF-7 in public databases,” he adds.

Before posting his preprint, David began flagging the anomalous protein-expression cases on the post-publication peer-review site PubPeer. Some journals are taking action. At least five of the papers have been retracted, three corrected and four now have an expression of concern. At least one other is marked as under investigation on the journal website.

These papers are not the first to be retracted owing to complications with cell lines, Soussi notes. Several practices that are common in laboratories increase the risk of contamination, he says. Cell lines are often passed between lab members who might not know where the cells originally came from, and several cell lines can be handled at the same time.

This means that the presence of impossible protein patterns in papers will probably remain a recurring matter, indicates Soussi. “As long as human nature does not change, it will persist.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • To the background buzz of Australian cricket ripping itself apart over sandpapergate, England kick off their T20 series at the same venue they became world champions four years ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports.

The international break is over as domestic football boogies back. Primed to feel the force is Dominic Booth at the helm of our essential gateway to the weekend’s action. Saturday offers a magnificent seven Premier League matches, bookended by Manchester City v Fulham and Newcastle v Arsenal. There is also a full programme of Championship, League One, and League Two fixtures, plus Celtic and Rangers taking to the Glasgow greensward in Scotland. In the WSL, Liverpool host Chelsea before rich kids London City prepare to receive Crystal Palace. For breaking news, reader input and good vibes aplenty – join the conversation at matchday.live@theguardian.com.

To the background buzz of Australian cricket ripping itself apart over sandpapergate, England kick off their T20 series at the same venue they became world champions four years ago. The Melbourne Cricket Ground has not always been a happy hunting ground for touring England sides but Harry Brook’s last two visits as captain have been triumphant. A two-day win at the 90,000-capacity venue in last year’s Boxing Day Test was not only the high point of a traumatic Ashes campaign; it was their first red-ball victory on Australian soil since 2011. MCG also hosted England’s T20 World Cup triumph in 2022, where Brook was part of the side that defeated Pakistan to lift the trophy behind enemy lines. Rob Smyth has over-by-over coverage with Ali Martin reporting from Melbourne.

The lunchtime kick-off is a vital one for the hosts. City have wobbled of late, three straight Premier League defeats leave the beleaguered club in third with 21 points from the first 10 games of Enzo Maresca’s tenure. In stark contrast, the Cottagers are unbeaten in their last four games, after four defeats and two draws in their first six. Wins over Hull and Coventry came before draws with Aston Villa and Newcastle. Barry Glendenning helms the blog as Will Unwin reports from the Etihad Stadium.

England are have been transformed since stumbling through the Six Nations and then falling to South Africa at Ellis Park, winning four consecutive Tests, amassing 36 tries and addressing their disciplinary lapses. Aided by thumping victories over Fiji and Japan, they have rebuilt impressively to secure a shot at reaching the Nations Championship final, but Latest Zealand provide the true measure of their progress. Only South Africa are higher in the rankings and a year out from the 2027 World Cup final, it is the opportunity for Steve Borthwick’s men to make a statement. Lee Calvert blogs the action and the trio of Robert Kitson, Andy Bull and Gerard Meagher making up our Twickenham reporting team.

Sources indicate that katy Murrells is at the controls of our tennis liveblog as the semi-finals pan out in Turin. The first session starts at 2.30pm, with the evening match due to start at about 8.30pm.

Recent findings suggest that emillia Hawkins keeps the updates flowing on the five afternoon kick-offs: Aston Villa v Sunderland, Bournemouth v Nottingham Forest, Chelsea v Leeds, Coventry v Crystal Palace, and Tottenham v Ipswich – the pick of the bunch. Roberto De Zerbi seemed to be making an impact at Spurs before a defeat by Leeds tripped up his side. Their record is grim against the Tractor Boys: four defeats in their last five Premier league games.

Lee Calvert is back on deck as Ireland risk a Springbok backlash from a side bruised by defeat by France and furious at their coach, Rassie Erasmus, for getting banned after his incendiary “match-fixing” comments. Supernova explodes before astronomers' eyes | Space photo of the day for Nov. 18, 2026

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (462 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new supernova has been spotted exploding in the spiral galaxy NGC 1433, about 50 million light-years from Earth.
  • In a recent development, researchers have discovered a new supernova called SN 2026ahvu.
  • During most type Ia supernovae, the white dwarf pulls material away from the other star until enough accumulates on its surface to create an explosion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new supernova has been spotted exploding in the spiral galaxy NGC 1433, about 50 million light-years from Earth.

In a recent development, researchers have discovered a new supernova called SN 2026ahvu. A Type Ia supernova, this event took place in a system with two stars orbiting one another (also known as a binary system), in which typically one star is an exploding white dwarf.

During most type Ia supernovae, the white dwarf pulls material away from the other star until enough accumulates on its surface to create an explosion.

Finding galaxies where stellar explosions are taking place isn't a rarity. However, this supernova is unique in how early it was captured. If the supernova were starting to dim, researchers might infer that the event was ending. However, according to details shared when it was first spotted, as well as later observations, this supernova was discovered while getting brighter.

This indicates that the supernova was likely caught early in the process of exploding, providing researchers with a unique opportunity to observe the event as it is taking place. By exploring observations of the galaxy before, during and (in the future) after the supernova event, researchers can investigate this type Ia supernova and how it affected the system in which it took place.

Scientists made this discovery using ATLAS, or the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact System, which is a robotic astronomical survey made up of telescopes across both hemispheres.

It has been revealed that ATLAS is designed to spot incoming near-Earth objects like asteroids before they can reach Earth. It's essentially an asteroid impact early warning system.

Recent findings suggest that but just because that's what the system is designed for doesn't mean that's all it can do. The system can also spot other objects moving through space and, in this instance, it was able to capture observations of this supernova.

Following its initial discovery, other observations of the supernova were made using NOIRLab's Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and Gemini South telescope.

According to recent reports, chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. You can follow her online @chelsea.gohd and @foxanne.music.

#59335. ‘The Hairiest 90 Minutes of My Career’: How the FAA Ground Stop Went Down

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1188 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

‘The Hairiest 90 Minutes of My Career’: How the FAA Ground Stop Went Down

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that by Wednesday of this week—six days after a 4.5-hour nationwide ground stop that panicked onlookers and scrambled air travel—US transportation secretary Sean Duffy remarked he still wasn’t quite sure what led to the Friday meltdown.
  • Industry observers note that still, the Federal Aviation Administration has revealed that a few things did go wrong on Friday afternoon.
  • The agency has since described the ground stop as something executed “out of an abundance of caution.” On Wednesday, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford appeared to downplay the incident even as he took blame for it, calling the outage “a knee scrape, and I’m sorry.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that by Wednesday of this week—six days after a 4.5-hour nationwide ground stop that panicked onlookers and scrambled air travel—US transportation secretary Sean Duffy remarked he still wasn’t quite sure what led to the Friday meltdown. “The root cause of what happened, we don’t have clarity yet,” he said after a meeting with lawmakers.

Industry observers note that still, the Federal Aviation Administration has revealed that a few things did go wrong on Friday afternoon. It involved routine infrastructure replacement, a faulty router, data overload, and disruption in some regions in the radio communications that air traffic controllers use to speak to each other and pilots.

The agency has since described the ground stop as something executed “out of an abundance of caution.” On Wednesday, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford appeared to downplay the incident even as he took blame for it, calling the outage “a knee scrape, and I’m sorry.”.

While aviation industry workers maintain that flyers were safe throughout the ground stop, some felt government officials downplayed the event, which left air traffic controllers scrambling to backup frequencies even as they tried to figure out what was going on.

“That was the hairiest 90 minutes of my career,” one air traffic controller told WIRED.

Contacted for comment, FAA spokesperson Steve Kulm didn't answer questions but referred WIRED to the agency’s ground stop Q&A web page, where the agency writes it has “clear, established, standard procedures to ensure safety during incidents such as this.” It says that some radio frequencies and radar feeds remained online during the communication challenges, “allowing air traffic controllers to maintain communication with and track aircraft.”.

Here’s what we know about the ground stop so far.

To understand the communications issues that led to the ground stop, here’s a quick overview on how air traffic control works.

Most flyers are familiar with the towers near airports, officially called the Airport Traffic Control Towers (ATCT). The controllers who work here manage aircraft ground movements, including takeoffs and landings. Once an aircraft gets up into the sky, around 10,000 feet, it’s passed to controllers in a Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON) center, who manage airport arrivals and departures. Then, once a flight is really underway, an aircraft is passed to Air Route Traffic Control Centers, often just called Centers. There are 22 of these in the US, and controllers there guide airplanes for most of their flight, passing off the aircraft as they move between regions.

The communication radios used at Centers have a range of around 150 miles—a problem when the areas they have to manage are more than 100,000 square miles each. So phone lines at the Centers lead to networks of transmitters, each installed remotely.

For decades, this network has been connected by copper telecommunications lines—outdated and sometimes brittle tech. So in 2025’s GOP-led Big Beautiful Bill, the Transportation Department received the billions of dollars in funding needed to upgrade that copper to fiber-optic cables. The upgrade swaps the system, the private communications backbone of Air Traffic Control, from one of mechanical switches to a digital system built on internet-based protocols. A contractor called L3Harris—the network owner—manages the transition, and as of last week, the project was about 70 percent complete. This was where the FAA ran into problems.

The trouble began in El Dorado, Arkansas, the site of one of those remote communications facilities, which is part of the larger Center based in Memphis, Tennessee. There, the FAA indicates a contractor with L3Harris was making on Friday what is now a routine switch from that legacy copper system to a fiber-optic one. But something, it appears, went wrong when the worker plugged in a upcoming router as part of that transition, and the FAA still doesn’t know why.

Data began to flood the network, making 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds, according to the FAA. The agency claims another remote site, a radar-based facility in Amarillo, Texas, may have also flooded the network with data. To compensate, the network tried to recruit other nodes, and they got overloaded, too, taking down several radio frequencies on the network.

It has been revealed that at first, the issue manifested as intermittent dropouts on radio frequencies at Centers in the region, from Kansas City to Chicago, according to two people familiar with the matter who spoke to WIRED under the condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak to the press. This made it difficult, if not impossible, for air traffic controllers to talk between Centers and with pilots through normal channels. From there, though, the issues seem to have cascaded to other regions, including the areas around Washington, DC, and New York.

In control rooms—mostly Centers dealing with en route flights—air traffic controllers first noticed some “dropouts” on their radio transmissions, according to two sources. On their own, these sorts of communication disruptions aren’t unheard of. But when they began to spread to multiple regions, FAA officials really began to pay attention.

Because officials didn’t understand why the radio frequencies were unstable, the agency called a nationwide ground stop.

According to recent reports, one person who spoke with WIRED stated they still had access to a backup frequency during the network instability. The FAA said “some frequencies and radar feeds remained reliable.”.

Recent findings suggest that then, according to the FAA, contractors from L3 Harris blocked data from the remote Arkansas and Texas locations from the wider network. That restabilized the system, restoring radio contact between everyone in the airspace.

In a statement Friday, a spokesperson for the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, a union that represents almost 20,000 controllers, wrote that “air traffic controllers were on the job, carrying out their responsibilities and working to ensure the safety of the National Airspace System.”.

Sources indicate that while the technical problems led to several uncomfortable hours for aviation professionals, midair passengers remained safe during the ground stop, indicates Scott Miller, an airline pilot and a lecturer in the Aviation and Technology program at San Jose State University in California. “It was certainly an abnormal situation, but it wasn’t an emergency, because we’ve trained for it,” he says. “It was not dangerous, but it was highly inconveniencing, and it was not normal.”.

It helped that the radio outage did not seem to have affected all Centers, and even fewer TRACONs and local towers. That means pilots were generally in contact with controllers, especially as they circled airports and landed their planes.

In a recent development, it also helped that pilots don’t actually need air traffic control to fly their planes, Miller notes. “Talking to a controller is not what keeps an airplane in the sky,” he says. Pilots have plenty of systems onboard that allow them to “see” what’s going on around them.

It has been revealed that despite the lack of clarity on what exactly happened with the newly installed router to make it malfunction, Duffy has settled on a solution: more money. On Wednesday, he officially asked Congress for $50 billion, with $30 billion of that dedicated to air traffic control modernization.

Bruce Willis’ wife, Emma Heming Willis, has celebrated their elder daughter’s birthday with a trip down memory lane.

Mabel Willis turned 11 on Sunday, and her proud mom marked the occasion by sharing a montage of family photos and videos taken over the years, set to the song “Pictures Of You” by The Cure.

“Happy 11th Birthday Mabel Ray!” Heming Willis wrote in the caption.

Emma Heming Willis speaks out about finding community as a caregiver: 'This journey can feel very dark'.

“Your energy is infectious,” she continued, praising her little girl for the way she “can light a whole room with your smile and warmth.”.

“How you love and care for your family and friends is beautiful to witness. Keep shining my love and always remember to #liveitup,” Heming Willis added.

According to recent reports, heming Willis and Willis married in 2009. Along with Mabel, the couple also have an 8-year-old daughter, Evelyn. Willis also has daughters Rumer, Scout and Tallulah with his ex-wife, Demi Moore.

Sources indicate that willis is clearly a doting dad. One picture in Heming Willis’ montage reveals the “Die Hard” star holding baby Mabel while planting a kiss on her forehead, while a more recent image shows a beaming Willis hanging out in nature with his preteen.

Bruce Willis sings with his family in birthday tribute video from ex Demi Moore.

According to recent reports, heming Willis penned an equally heartfelt tribute last month when her husband celebrated his 68th birthday. Sharing a video montage on Instagram, she referred to the actor as “pure love.”.

In February, Willis’ family declared that his speaking disorder, aphasia, had progressed into a form of dementia called frontotemporal dementia, or FTD.

“Today there are no treatments for the disease, a reality that we hope can change in the years ahead,” they said in an update shared online. “As Bruce’s condition advances, we hope that any media attention can be focused on shining a light on this disease that needs far more awareness and research.”.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, FTD refers to “a group of disorders caused by progressive nerve cell loss in the brain’s frontal lobes (the areas behind your forehead) or its temporal lobes.” These areas of the brain are generally associated with personality, behavior and language.

First defeat and first red for Ferguson as Glentoran falter

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ferguson was sent off in just his fourth game as Glentoran manager.
  • It was a night of unfortunate firsts for Duncan Ferguson at Solitude on Friday.
  • The Everton great suffered his first defeat as Glentoran boss as they were edged out 3-2 by Cliftonville in an Irish Premiership thriller.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ferguson was sent off in just his fourth game as Glentoran manager.

It was a night of unfortunate firsts for Duncan Ferguson at Solitude on Friday.

The Everton great suffered his first defeat as Glentoran boss as they were edged out 3-2 by Cliftonville in an Irish Premiership thriller.

He also received his first red card as a manager, after picking up nine during his playing career, in the first half for protesting the decision to award Cliftonville's first goal after he perceived a foul in the build-up.

The defeat ended Glentoran's eight-game unbeaten run in the league and leaves them well off the pace in pursuit of their first league title since 2009.

While he has delivered with his animated touchline antics, Ferguson has so far struggled to get much out of his side on the pitch.

Ferguson sent off as Reds beat Glens in thriller - report and highlights.

Highlights: Cliftonville v Glentoran.

The Glens were second best for much of the first half in north Belfast, with Cliftonville dominating possession and creating the better chances.

Still, the awarding of the Reds' first goal was controversial as it looked like defender Jarlath O'Rourke had been pushed by Liam McStravick, who then teed up Joe Sheridan to score the opener on 38 minutes.

Ferguson was incensed that the goal stood, protesting while his side went up the other end and scored an equaliser through Cal Weatherup's deflected strike a minute later.

Such was the vehemence of his words towards the officials, referee Ben McMaster brandished a straight red card and Ferguson was forced to make the long walk to the tunnel all while being jeered by Cliftonville supporters.

"I think the manager got frustrated because it was a foul. It changes the dynamic [the sending off], he's a leader, I've then got to step in and fill his boots and it's a major set of boots to fill," said Ferguson's assistant Gary Bollan.

His side looked to have received a stern talking to from Bollan at half-time as they were much more competitive after the break.

They responded to Brian Healy putting the Reds ahead once again with a fine James Douglas strike on 86 minutes, which looked to be enough to secure a point and continue their unbeaten run.

However, they failed to stop midfielder Sheridan, who waltzed into the box before firing into the top corner two minutes later to seal a win.

Glentoran's fifth league defeat of the campaign leaves them 14 points behind pacesetters Linfield.

Former Crusaders captain Colin Coates, who was on co-commentary duties for the game for BBC Sport NI, believes Ferguson and the club have "a lot of work to do" to get back challenging for major honours.

"Look at the squad, there is work to do in January and next summer," he added.

"Duncan Ferguson will use this next few months to assess what he has, what he wants to keep and what he needs to bring in to make them competitive. Every time I watch them I want more from them.

It has been revealed that "There is a real lack of quality particularly at the top end they don't look like they can hurt teams aside from Jordan Stewart. A lot of work and soul searching to do and players will be playing for their futures.".

Stewart was suspended for the game at Solitude and was a big miss while Ferguson will hope to get more out of Conor McMenamin and the fit-again Pat Hoban, who both came on in the second half.

The Glens face two games against Larne, one in the BetMcLean Cup on Tuesday and one in the league next Friday and Ferguson will hope to mastermind two big results to really kick-start his reign.

Sheridan scored two fine goals in Cliftonville's victory.

For Cliftonville, it was a case of another massive performance under the lights on a Friday in front of a raucous Solitude crowd.

The Reds beat Larne 4-2 at the same venue a fortnight ago and key in their two major wins in recent weeks has been teenage midfielder Sheridan, who is growing in stature for Jim Magilton.

The 19-year-old broke into the senior squad last season after a fruitful six-month spell at Queen's University in the 2024-25 campaign.

He won the club's Young Player of the Year award last season and was a rotation option, but he has kicked on again this year and firmly established himself in a midfield three with captain Rory Hale and Dean McMaster.

The next step for the talented Northern Ireland under-21 international is adding goals and assists to his game and he certainly delivered on Friday.

Former Glentoran captain Paul Leeman mentioned he showed "composure" for both his goals, first to curl home from close range, then to weave his way into the box and place the ball in the top corner.

According to recent reports, "It was a really good performance from him. He's becoming a mainstay in the team," Leeman added.

The victory moves Cliftonville to within a point of the Glens and with games against struggling Ballymena United and Bangor to come, they will hope to embark upon another winning run to continue their surge up the table.

#59329. UK Privy Council overrules Trinidad and Tobago gay sex law

UK Privy Council overrules Trinidad and Tobago gay sex law

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A man from Trinidad and Tobago has won a legal appeal lasting almost a decade in the last court of appeal available to him — the judicial committee of the Privy Council in former colonial power Britain.
  • Jason Jones, a gay man born in Trinidad and Tobago, had challenged the Caribbean nation's Sexual Offences Act outlawing consensusal sex between adult males, saying that it breached his fundamental rights under the country's constitution.
  • He initially won his case at Trinidad and Tobago's High Court, but the government and religious organizations managed to partially overturn the ruling once more, prompting Jones to the take the case to the island nation's highest appellate authority — the Privy Council in  the UK.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A man from Trinidad and Tobago has won a legal appeal lasting almost a decade in the last court of appeal available to him — the judicial committee of the Privy Council in former colonial power Britain.

Jason Jones, a gay man born in Trinidad and Tobago, had challenged the Caribbean nation's Sexual Offences Act outlawing consensusal sex between adult males, saying that it breached his fundamental rights under the country's constitution.

He initially won his case at Trinidad and Tobago's High Court, but the government and religious organizations managed to partially overturn the ruling once more, prompting Jones to the take the case to the island nation's highest appellate authority — the Privy Council in  the UK.

"To discriminate against somebody simply because of who they choose to love is simply ridiculous," Jones told the Associated Press after Tuesday's judgment was rendered.

The Privy Council in London is the final court of appeal for some Commonwealth countries including Trinidad and Tobago, although that glitch was already contentious in some circles prior to Tuesday's ruling.

A panel of five judges unanimously allowed Jones' appeal, dismissing a counter-appeal from the Caribbean country's Attorney General.

It found that two sections of the country's Sexual Offenses Act 1986, criminalizing "buggery" and "serious indecency" respectively among same-sex couples, violated Jones' fundamental rights to private and family life set out in the 1976 constitution.

The court wrote in its ruling that "the rights and interests of Mr Jones which are at stake involve a particularly important facet of his existence and identity since the ability to form an intimate and loving relationship with another person lies at the core of the right to private and family life.".

The anti-gay laws that call for up to five years in prison have not been enforced in recent history, but critics say they still send an intimidating message.

Judge Philip Sales remarked as he announced the ruling that "the current understanding of the fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life is that it protects such a core part of human identity as one's sexual orientation.".

Sales added that "laws which seek to criminalize such activities cannot be justified.".

Trinidadian authorities argued that because the 1986 laws were passed with a super-majority and constituted criminal penalties that dated back to colonial times, prior to the constitution, they could be considered "existing law" and override the individual constitutional rights in certain circumstances.

But the Privy Council judges found that the so-called "proviso" for this special status — "unless the Act is shown not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual" — had not been met.

One of Jones' lawyers, Anand Ramlogan, is a former attorney general of Trinidad and Tobago and argued against this position earlier in the case.

Recent findings suggest that "Constitutional rights exist precisely because majorities are not always right," Ramlogan remarked. "They ensure that the dignity and equality of every citizen are not left to the changing tides of public opinion.".

Jason Jones is a 61-year-old born in Trinidad and Tobago.

Openly gay since the age of 16, he mentioned he fled the country in 1996 because of homophobic violence and discrimination.

Speaking to the Associated Press on Tuesday after what he termed a "stunning victory," he stated he would describe himself as a "very angry gay man," whose anger had helped him persist in his legal appeal for so many years.

"Society has treated me worse than a criminal," he remarked. "There is a real sense of vindication with this judgment. Finally, the courts are seeing that they need to step up because our politicians are so toothless.".

He mentioned he became inspired to speak out after losing friends to HIV/AIDS and after meeting American singer-songwriter Nina Simone when she toured the island nation for three weeks in 1984, when he was 19.

"Nina was the one who mentioned, 'Jason, get off this rock and go see the world,'" he said, calling it a defining and life-changing experience.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Trinidad and Tobago's government, the country's Council of Evangelical Churches and its largest Hindu organization, Sanatan Dharm Maha Sabha, contested the case, which has wound its way through several courts since the appeal was introduced in 2017.

In 2018, Trinidad's High Court found the laws unconstitutional. But in 2025, a local appeals court partially reversed the ruling. Trinidad's Court of Appeals subsequently allowed Jones to seek a ruling from the final appeals court in England.

The case was being closely watched by activists across the Caribbean, with similar laws in place in several other countries in the region.

The Bahamas decriminalized homosexuality in 1991.

The UK repealed laws in overseas territories Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands in 2001.

Sources indicate that judges in Barbados, Dominica, St. Lucia and Antigua and Barbuda have also recently struck down similar laws.

Sources indicate that but in former British colonies Grenada, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago and St. Vincent and the Grenadines it remains a crime.

Recent findings suggest that the UK only decriminalized gay sex in 1967, more than four centuries after the so-called "buggery" laws were first introduced under King Henry VII, and more than a century after the last executions for the crime. People still faced prosecution or the threat of it for consensual adult gay sex until after World War II, with surely the most famous later-years case being that of computing and codebreaking pioneer and war hero Alan Turing.

Germany forward on her latest life in London and drawing strength from the memory of her late brother, Dennis.

Sources indicate that lisa Baum is 19, for the next few days at least, but you wouldn’t know it. The Germany forward plays with a maturity that explains why she was handed her Arsenal debut in their opening game of the season, less than two months after joining.

It has been revealed that baum had been told that the 2025 European champions had a vision for her but that coming in as a young player she would have to be patient. Ten minutes into her debut against Brighton, in Crawley, the young winger scored what would be the winning goal.

“It was unbelievable,” claims Baum, speaking in a small meeting room at Arsenal’s London Colney training ground with a maturity that matches her play. “Everything just went so quick. I just shot, my brain was just switched off, it just came out.”.

Sources indicate that that win kickstarted Arsenal’s season but it quickly stalled. In the league, the team went five games without a win. After a 2-0 defeat by OL Lyonnes in the Champions League on Thursday night, Arsenal have five wins from their opening 15 games. It is far from the season they, or many others, envisaged.

Sunday’s final home game of the year, against West Ham, offers an opportunity to take some positivity into the international break, after which Arsenal face three away fixtures before the winter pause.

“I believe in us,” claims Baum. “I think it’s all about the small margins. Sometimes it’s luck, sometimes it’s in the final decision-making, sometimes it’s how close we are to a goal that doesn’t go in. But we work really hard in every training session and on trying to keep ourselves up mentally and physically. We’re trying to push through the barrier that we maybe have right now, but we get a lot of trust from the staff and coaches. Everybody really believes in each other and I think it’s not going to take long before we’re through this part of the journey.”.

Industry observers note that overall, Arsenal have not been playing particularly badly. They have been creating chances and dominating games but struggling to translate that into goals and points. In October, Baum earned a first senior Germany call-up and made her debut off the bench at half-time against Australia, having previously featured for teams from the under-16s to under-23s.

The Liverpool head coach, Gareth Taylor, indicates Pro Ref has accepted it made an error in disallowing a goal his side thought they had scored during this month's 2-1 defeat by Arsenal at Anfield.

Industry observers note that the Women’s Super League game was level at 1-1 when Jenna Clark tucked the ball into the net after ­Arsenal had failed to clear a corner, but the assistant referee disallowed the goal for offside against Vivien ­Endemann. Replays highlighted the delivery had been ­inadvertently played off an Arsenal foot rather than being a deliberate forward pass from the home side. There is no VAR in the WSL.

In a recent development, taylor, whose side host Chelsea in the WSL on Saturday, said on Friday: “We have had an acceptance of a mistake from the corner that we scored from, where we should be 2-1 up at half-time. [There was] no apology, but we accept that there was an error made on their part and that game can look different.” Tom Garry.

Baum moved to Germany when she was four. Born to a Tanzanian mother and German father, she spent her first years in Dar es Salaam in Tanzania. They swapped a city with a population of about four million for Ahrensbök, a municipality with a population of just over 8,000 near the Baltic coast. “I think my mum had the hardest time out of us in the family, with the move to Germany,” she states. Baum says she and her brother, Dennis, “learned to adapt easily”.

Recent findings suggest that baum doesn’t remember her years on the east coast of Africa but when she went back three or four years ago, some sort of memory was triggered. “It was a feeling, or feelings,” she claims. “It was so good to grow up there. It was warm, it was the beautiful beaches, it was having all your family around. I was in kindergarten or I was in the water a lot – I love to swim.”.

She started playing football after the move to northern Germany, desperate to copy Dennis. “My father played football when he was younger – he was a goalkeeper – but he stopped when he didn’t really enjoy it any more. My mum wasn’t a substantial fan of me playing; she dressed me like a girly girl, with princess dresses and that kind of stuff, but I was never really like that at that age. I always wanted to follow my older brother – I wanted to wear his clothes. He started playing football before me and I wanted to be like him.”.

Baum would play on the side of the pitch at her brother’s club until a parent said she should be playing too. After playing with various local teams she joined Hamburg’s academy. She worked her way into the first team and they won promotion to the second tier in her first season. In the 2024-25 season they reached the DFB-Pokal semi-finals and the top flight. Baum moved to RB Leipzig and scored five goals in 27 games before Arsenal swooped.

“Everything was just so quick,” she says of the move to London. Training required getting used to: “Everything was so sharp, everything was technically excellent, like 10 out of 10. I was quite nervous and had some clumsy actions.”.

In a recent development, the transfer also involved swapping an average attendance last season of 1,651 for one of 33,808. “It’s unbelievable,” notes Baum of playing at the Emirates Stadium. “I had only played in a substantial stadium once before. You can’t even believe how much the fans give you when you step on the pitch. There’s so much support, that of course we need in this current time. I think Arsenal is a club that holds on to us, on to the team, and gives us a lot of strength.”.

According to recent reports, look closely at Baum’s left wrist when she plays and you will usually see a strip of white tape around it. Sometimes it has something written on it. She’s done it “since that day” – the day in 2022 when Dennis died in a car accident, aged 17.

The brother that inspired her on to a pitch is with her on it at the highest level. “The next time I was on the football pitch, I just felt I wanted to do that,” she claims. “I feel like it’s given me a different kind of strength and confidence. Sometimes I don’t write anything, but it’s about just having the physical feeling that he is with me.”.

What history tells us about the Premier League table after 10 games of a season
