Argentinian has excelled in man-management – but will need his powers to energise new squad and impress owners.

It has been revealed that mauricio Pochettino celebrated his 50th birthday in style. It was March 2022, he was in charge at Paris Saint-Germain and the venue was a stunning boutique hotel; the kind that many capitals have but only Paris truly does. Pochettino’s family and friends were there. So were his inner coaching circle, who are basically family. There were lots of people from PSG. And a good time was had by all.

In a recent development, for Pochettino, it was emotional. As everybody knows, the new Manchester United head coach is the kind of guy to well up when the speeches start, so imagine how he felt when he looked up at the big screen and a video montage of well-wishers started to roll.

In a recent development, pochettino’s PSG players were at the party. There was no need for anything from them. But there were loads from those he had coached at his previous clubs: Espanyol, Southampton and Tottenham. One by one, the faces flashed up; too many to mention. And, of course, there were the jokes about how old he was getting. But the tone was of pure affection; appreciation, too. Some of the players laid it on thick. They could not help it. They know what Pochettino has done for them.

This is what total buy-in looks like and this is how Pochettino gets you when he finds out which buttons to press. It might be a third-choice goalkeeper. Or a global superstar – for example, Kylian Mbappé, who Pochettino had at PSG. There is a story from those days that is worth sharing. Pochettino was due to give an interview and told the TV crew he would get Mbappé along to speak to them as well.

Recent findings suggest that everybody knows this is not how it works, that it would not be possible because Mbappé, well … he has his time and commitments tightly managed. They appreciated the sentiment from Pochettino, though. When the hour came, Pochettino took out his phone and messaged Mbappé. “Come to the media centre.” Five minutes later, there he was. A line from one of the production staff was gold. “Err, we’ve got Kylian Mbappé outside.”.

This kind of thing is not confined to the dim and distant past. Remember when Pochettino left Chelsea in 2024 and the tributes some of the players paid to him on social media? One stood out because it came from Nicolas Jackson, who Pochettino had punished for getting too many silly yellow cards by ordering him to sprint around the training ground, reducing him to a face-in-the-ground mess when it was over. “Love you coach,” Jackson wrote. “Thanks for the advice and support. You’re a true lion and a fighter.”.

It is easy to feel Pochettino has signed up for his biggest fight because it is not only that United have one Premier League win, a place in the relegation zone, no confidence, questionable fitness levels and a trip to Liverpool on Sunday which has the makings of root canal surgery without the anaesthetic.

It has been revealed that hanging heavy over everything is the fan fury towards the Glazer family, who have owned the club since 2005. It is obviously not a new thing. The diehards were passionately against them even before the takeover. But we are going through another period where the frustration has spiked and the malevolence can be heard in the chants. It is the insoluble problem, with the efforts of the minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the director of football, Jason Wilcox, making it worse. They have also been targeted by the Stretford End.

In a recent development, pochettino knows managers do not tend to enter clubs when everything is rosy. There are reasons why the vacancies arise and they are almost always bad. He has told himself this. What he intends to do is what he has always done: create connections, starting with the players; inject his trademark positivity into every pore; build belief.

The Argentinian is obsessed with what he calls energia universal. It is a guiding life force that influences everything, which touches on concepts such as karma and what these days would probably be called manifestation. He once said it helped to explain, for example, why the London-born Harry Kane usually scored for Spurs in London derbies.

Pochettino wants to release the pressure from United’s beleaguered squad and his early messaging has come from his tried and trusted playbook. Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Crows can make visual decisions twice as promptly as humans and monkeys, according to upcoming research from the University of Tübingen.
  • The findings, published in the journal Science, offer newly introduced insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions.
  • Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crows can make visual decisions twice as promptly as humans and monkeys, according to upcoming research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

The findings, published in the journal Science, offer newly introduced insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.

To test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

The birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent.".

According to recent reports, the results showed that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds.

Industry observers note that the team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an important role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

In a recent development, the recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

Industry observers note that these signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes.

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," notes Andreas Nieder.

Unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as quickly as primates.

The researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially key for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

However, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

#59272. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (955 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, you know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black?
  • Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?
  • Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, you know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Your brain has its own version of that.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

Recent findings suggest that but to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

Sources indicate that and they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a fresh task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in fresh ways.

Sources indicate that it turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

But it's crucial to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

According to recent reports, there's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?".

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

Sources indicate that in a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice notable signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

And the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

In a recent development, maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

The DMN is not always necessarily good.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great fresh idea.

In a recent development, but it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

It has been revealed that scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

According to recent reports, protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

Recent findings suggest that take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Embrace boredom and enjoy doing nothing.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

Try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

Industry observers note that you can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

Astronomers witness a star eating its companion in 1st-of-its-kind observation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a new study reports.
  • Recent findings suggest that as stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby.
  • "Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in New York, told Space.com.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a new study reports.

Recent findings suggest that as stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now.

"Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in New York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean. We need sensitive telescopes monitoring the sky for a long time in order to catch this effect.".

In the fresh study, the researchers investigated a red giant star designated WNTR23bzdiq, which is located about 2.5 million light-years away in the Andromeda galaxy. The star is about seven times heftier and 350 times wider than our own sun.

In 2023, using NASA's now-defunct NEOWISE space telescope and the WINTER telescope at Palomar Observatory in California, the scientists noticed that this star was brightening. By analyzing previous records, they found that the red giant had gradually started growing more luminous in 2018.

The researchers had previously suggested this brightening potentially occurred because the giant star engulfed a companion star. As this companion spiraled toward the giant's core, it would generate friction, heat and light, explaining the increasing luminosity.

In a recent development, then, near the end of 2025, the astronomers saw a giant eruption of light from this giant star. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope observed the star just 47 days after that eruption, allowing the team to characterize the event in detail. The researchers now propose that this explosion happened when a companion star about 70% the sun's mass rammed into the giant's heart.

"I was absolutely flabbergasted when we saw this," Karambelkar mentioned.

In the latest study, the scientists estimated that the eruption expelled an amount of material equal to about 0.1 to 0.2 times the mass of the sun. "Stars engulfing their companions have been theorized for many decades, and this event provides the first observations of this theoretical prediction," Karambelkar mentioned.

Although these findings suggest that two stars — a binary system nicknamed "Bao" — merged into one, "it is not the only possibility," Karambelkar noted. "The other possibility is that both stars survived, in a much shorter orbit. In order to conclusively determine what happened, we need to continue monitoring what the system does, once the heft of the eruption settles down.".

Now that astronomers may have found the first such merger, "I can't wait to find more," Karambelkar said. "Upcoming telescopes like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Vera Rubin Observatory will be very useful in discovering many more such events.".

Industry observers note that the scientists detailed their findings Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

England forward injured in Friday’s 1-1 draw with Cologne.

Club statement confirms ‘tear of ligament in left ankle’.

Bayern Munich have confirmed Harry Kane will be “out for the next few months” with ankle ligament damage sustained in their 1-1 draw with Cologne on Friday.

Kane was substituted after 20 minutes of the Bundesliga game, having been left limping after a challenge from the Cologne defender Joël Schmied. The Ballon d’Or winner was substituted with the returning Bayern coach, Vincent Kompany, saying afterwards that the injury would take “months” rather than weeks to heal.

A club statement on X said: “Harry Kane suffered a tear of the syndesmosis ligament in his left ankle in Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga home match against Köln on Friday evening. This was confirmed by an examination by Bayern Munich’s medical department. The 33-year-old will therefore be out for the next few months.”.

Industry observers note that the Tottenham loanee Mikey Moore fired the visitors ahead before Kane’s injury, but Bayern levelled things up when Nathaniel Brown scored before the break. Bayern also lost Michael Olise to injury for the second half, and Said El Mala missed an excellent late chance to earn Cologne’s first win at Bayern since 2009.

The 33-year-old may face a race to be fit for the Nations League quarter-finals, with the first leg in Norway taking place on 27 March – just over four months away. The Bayern sporting director, Max Eberl, stated on Friday that club doctors were “at the moment discussing whether or not to recommend surgery” for Kane’s injury.

In a recent development, part of Kane’s recovery period will come during the Bundesliga’s winter break from 20 December to 8 January. He will, however, miss Champions League games away to Lille next week and at home to Slavia Prague next month, as well as the January trip to Manchester United and the league phase finale at home to Real Betis.

According to recent reports, kane’s setback adds to an extensive Bayern injury list, with Michael Olise also going off during Friday’s game with a foot contusion. Luis Díaz, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, Ismael Saibari and Manuel Neuer were already unavailable, leaving Kompany short of options for a busy month of fixtures.

Industry observers note that kompany returned from his own month-long absence for Friday’s game with his arm in a sling, having dislocated his shoulder when he collapsed on a training pitch in October. The Belgian was taken to hospital for meningeal irritation treatment after his collapse, and has been recovering at home.

Cologne took a surprise lead with 12 minutes gone as Moore started and finished an excellent break. The teenage winger pounced on a mislaid Olise pass and drove forward, finding Linton Maina who laid off for El Mala, whose no-look backheel pass allowed Moore to round keeper Jonas Urbig before sliding the ball home.

Industry observers note that kane was then brought down in the Cologne box from behind by defender Schmied, who got the ball first but clattered into Kane’s left leg in his follow-through. Kane’s penalty appeals were waved away, but he was left visibly limping and received treatment on his ankle before being replaced by Tom Bischof on the 20-minute mark.

The hosts levelled 17 minutes later as full-back Brown sliced a low shot into the bottom-right corner, but suffered another blow just before the break when Olise went down. The France star did not return to the field for the second half, and was seen leaving the stadium shortly after on crutches – but it appears unlikely he will miss a significant amount of time.

Sources indicate that just before the hour mark, El Mala and Maina forced a spectacular double save from Urbig just before the hour mark. Since arriving from Tottenham three years ago, Kane has bagged an incredible 156 goals in 163 appearances, helping Bayern win a league and cup double last season.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google and Apple might be competitors, but they can play nice sometimes.

For example, Google just announced that you can now use Gemini AI to control a Mac computer. With this newly introduced feature, you can give Gemini commands and it will root through your files, access your apps, and browse the web to complete whatever tasks you've asked it to perform. All of this is facilitated by the Gemini app for macOS 27 Golden Gate, per Google's press release.

How can owners take advantage of Gemini computer use for MacBooks, Mac Mini, and iMac devices?

Google provided several examples in an announcement blog post, such as asking Gemini to take a child's sketch of a butterfly and render it polygonally using the 3D modeling program Blender. Once the request is processed, Gemini performs the task in an isolated background window with a preview display right in the Gemini app, allowing you to watch it perform the task in real-time. However, as Google noted, you also retain full use of your Mac while this is happening, allowing consumers to continue browsing, typing, and completing other types of work.

While this may be a boon to Gemini power customers who own devices like the fresh MacBook Pro OLED, it's worth noting that giving an AI agent full access to all your local files and apps carries inherent risks. Google gives users the ability to freely choose which apps Gemini has access to, alongside the ability to watch the process as it unfolds, in case something goes wrong. So, you can pause Gemini if it's doing something you don't like, and approve decisions before they're made. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

It should also be noted that Google is playing catch-up with this announcement. Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic already offer this type of agentic feature, so Google's just a tad late to the party.

Google also just upgraded Gemini with even more task-completing power this week, introducing Gemini Tasks, a feature in the AI chatbot that lets it complete tasks for browser consumers (a feature not to be confused with Google Tasks).

Per Google, the new computer use feature is rolling out immediately for English users in the Gemini app, though it requires a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. Users will need a Mac device with Apple Silicon and macOS Sequoia 15.0 or later.

To get started, visit gemini.google/mac.

Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1622 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for decades, scientists have generally assumed that dark energy, the mysterious component thought to be responsible for the Universe's accelerating expansion, has remained constant throughout cosmic history.
  • Industry observers note that researchers at Istanbul Technical University (ITU) have explored that possibility by taking a fresh look at an established alternative theory of gravity.
  • In a recent development, the research was conducted within Akarsu's group at ITU, alongside postdoctoral researcher Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for decades, scientists have generally assumed that dark energy, the mysterious component thought to be responsible for the Universe's accelerating expansion, has remained constant throughout cosmic history. That long-standing assumption is now facing upcoming scrutiny. Observations from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), which is constructing the largest three-dimensional map of the Universe, suggest that dark energy's influence may have changed over billions of years. Although the evidence is not yet strong enough to establish a discovery, it has renewed interest in a fundamental question: Could dark energy evolve rather than remain constant?

Industry observers note that researchers at Istanbul Technical University (ITU) have explored that possibility by taking a fresh look at an established alternative theory of gravity. In a 2025 study published in Physical Review D, an international team led by Prof. Özgür Akarsu of ITU's Department of Physics investigated a mathematical possibility that previous researchers had largely overlooked. Their analysis revealed a surprising scenario in which the effective density of dark energy was negative during the Universe's early history before eventually becoming positive.

In a recent development, the research was conducted within Akarsu's group at ITU, alongside postdoctoral researcher Dr. N. Merve Uzun and doctoral student Bilal Bulduk. The team also collaborated with Prof. Nihan Katırcı of Doğuş University, who previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in Akarsu's group, and Prof. Antonio De Felice of Kyoto University's Yukawa Institute for Theoretical Physics, an internationally recognized center for theoretical physics.

An Overlooked Possibility in Einstein's Theory of Gravity.

According to recent reports, the discovery came from examining a part of an existing theory that had received relatively little attention. Rather than proposing an entirely fresh explanation for dark energy, the researchers revisited a framework known as teleparallel f(T) gravity.

In a recent development, einstein's general theory of relativity explains gravity through the curvature of spacetime. Teleparallel gravity takes a different mathematical approach, describing gravity through a property called torsion. Scientists have spent years studying modified versions of this framework to investigate whether gravity itself might account for the Universe's accelerating expansion.

Earlier investigations of an exponential form of teleparallel gravity had concentrated on one particular set of mathematical solutions. This approach reflected a familiar assumption inherited from general relativity: dark energy should always have a positive density.

Akarsu and his colleagues decided to investigate what would happen if that restriction were removed. By considering a previously neglected branch of the theory, they uncovered a substantially different picture of how the Universe might have evolved.

Dark Energy May Have Switched From Negative to Positive.

The team's calculations revealed that two distinct cosmic histories could emerge even when the Universe contains the same amount of matter today.

One mathematical solution closely resembles the standard model of cosmology. The other predicts that effective dark energy had a negative density in the distant past. According to this second possibility, the density reached zero at approximately redshift 1.5, corresponding to roughly 9.5 billion years ago, before becoming positive and remaining that way.

Recent findings suggest that what makes the result particularly interesting is that the researchers did not need to introduce an additional adjustable parameter to produce this behavior. Instead, the determining factor is related to the Universe's present matter density, which selects the mathematical branch. As a result, the model retains the same six cosmological parameters used in the standard ΛCDM model.

The theory also avoids an vital potential problem. Although it predicts behavior that differs from Einstein's gravity across enormous cosmic distances, its departures from general relativity become naturally suppressed in dense environments. This allows the alternative solution to remain compatible with the highly accurate measurements of gravity made throughout the Solar System.

A Possible Explanation for the Hubble Tension.

The latest findings build on years of research into whether dark energy could have changed sign during the Universe's history.

Akarsu and his collaborators previously developed a framework called the sign-switching ΛCDM (ΛsCDM) model. In this scenario, the cosmological constant changes from negative to positive several billion years after the Massive Bang.

It has been revealed that previous analyses found that a change in the sign of dark energy's density could agree with DESI observations while potentially reducing several unresolved disagreements in cosmology. One of the most significant is the Hubble tension, the persistent discrepancy between different methods of measuring the Universe's present expansion rate.

However, an vital question remained unanswered. What underlying physical process could cause dark energy to undergo such a reversal?

The latest research offers a possible mechanism. Instead of requiring scientists to prescribe a sign change as part of the model, the reversal arises naturally from the mathematical structure of the modified gravity theory.

Akarsu explained why investigating an overlooked solution proved so valuable.

Recent findings suggest that "For several years we have been studying a scenario in which dark energy switches sign, and it has held up remarkably well against data such as DESI's. The open question was what physical mechanism could produce such behavior. So we deliberately looked at a branch of a well-known theory of gravity that had been set aside because it violates the usual expectation that the dark energy density stays positive. The sign change emerged naturally from the theory itself.".

DESI Observations Raise Latest Questions About Dark Energy.

The theoretical findings have become especially relevant as astronomers gather increasingly detailed measurements of cosmic expansion.

DESI tracks the locations of millions of galaxies and quasars, allowing researchers to reconstruct how the Universe has expanded across billions of years. In March 2025, the DESI collaboration released findings based on its first three years of observations.

When combined with measurements of the cosmic microwave background, supernovae, and weak gravitational lensing, the results strengthened earlier indications that dark energy might not behave like a fixed cosmological constant.

Recent findings suggest that these findings do not yet establish that dark energy changes over time. The statistical significance depends on which observational datasets are combined, and the evidence remains below the threshold required to claim a definitive discovery. Nevertheless, the possibility has motivated scientists to investigate alternative descriptions of cosmic expansion.

DESI has now completed its planned five-year survey, observing more than 47 million galaxies and quasars. The complete dataset will provide an even more demanding test of whether the apparent changes in dark energy persist as measurements become more precise.

Industry observers note that the timing is also noteworthy. The ITU-led team's research was initially submitted in October 2024, several months before DESI revealed its March 2025 findings. The researchers have not yet tested their model against the complete DESI dataset, making that comparison an notable next step.

Could the Universe's Accelerating Expansion Be Slowing?

The significance of the proposed model extends beyond its prediction that dark energy's density may have changed sign.

In a recent development, because the alternative solution emerges from a specific theory of gravity, it makes predictions about both cosmic expansion and how gravity behaves across the Universe. These predictions give astronomers ways to investigate whether the proposed cosmic history is consistent with observations.

Measurements of how galaxies and larger structures form and grow will be particularly important. Researchers can also examine how gravity bends light and how the Universe's expansion has changed over time. Among the most useful observational tests are structure growth, redshift-space distortions, and weak gravitational lensing.

Although comprehensive testing remains necessary, the initial results offer reasons for further investigation.

In an extended version of the theory that includes a cosmological constant, the researchers found that the model could remain consistent with observations of the cosmic microwave background while allowing the higher present-day expansion rates obtained from local measurements. This makes it a potentially useful approach to understanding the Hubble tension.

According to recent reports, the extended model also permits another intriguing possibility: the acceleration of the Universe's expansion could have weakened or even stopped in the relatively recent cosmic past. Recent studies examining DESI observations have raised similar questions about whether cosmic acceleration has remained steady.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, neither the proposed dark energy reversal nor a recent slowdown in cosmic acceleration has been established as an observational fact. Both remain possibilities that must be tested against increasingly precise data.

Revisiting Gravity Could Reveal a Different Cosmic History.

The research highlights how familiar scientific theories can contain possibilities that were missed because earlier investigations relied on restrictive assumptions.

Industry observers note that in this case, allowing effective dark energy to have a negative density exposed an alternative evolutionary history within an already established mathematical framework. The researchers suggest that examining similarly overlooked solutions in other modified gravity theories could lead to additional insights.

Industry observers note that ultimately, the strength of the new explanation will depend on how well it reproduces the Universe astronomers actually observe. The full DESI dataset and other cosmological measurements will help determine whether this unusual version of cosmic history deserves a place alongside established explanations.

According to recent reports, "We identified an alternative path for the Universe within an existing theory. The next step is to test it rigorously against the full observational data. The preliminary picture is encouraging, and we are particularly interested in what it may tell us about the Hubble tension," said Prof. Özgür Akarsu.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A upcoming study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.
  • About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
  • Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC says.

In a recent development, cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the New York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC claims the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

According to recent reports, lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A upcoming study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

The researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort.

As lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s key to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

Further study is required, said study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

According to recent reports, “Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz said in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

Sources indicate that the implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

“If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”.

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic.

It has been revealed that dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

“It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the newly introduced research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”.

According to recent reports, other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

In a recent development, A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer stated. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

It has been revealed that “There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer stated. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”.

Lance Broadway, the former pitcher for the Chicago White Sox and New York Mets, died unexpectedly on Nov. 17, according to the Dallas County Medical Examiner's Office. He was 43.

The Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. actor died in an apartment complex stairwell in Dallas, Texas, public records confirm, though his cause of death is still pending autopsy results.

Broadway began his career in the spotlight with the Chicago baseball team when he was selected as the 15th overall pick at the 2005 MLB draft.

He spent two years in Triple-A—the highest level in Minor League Baseball—before making his Major League debut in 2007 as the White Sox's third-best prospect.

In a recent development, the Sox ultimately traded him to the Newly introduced York Mets for Ramón Castro two years later. After a few months back in the minors, he was called up to take over for Óliver Perez. But his time on the field didn't end in NYC. Broadway signed with the Toronto Blue Jays three months later to a minor-league deal, concluding his MLB career after a full season with the Triple-A Las Vegas 51s.

Though the former athlete threw his final pitch in 2010, he wasn't ready to bid farewell to the camera just yet. In fact, he went on to make his acting debut in 2011's Deadly Notes and Food Attack.

He then went on to star in Olympus Has Fallen (2013) as Agent O'Neil and played a TAC Team Leader in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.

Broadway previously revealed that transitioning to acting after concluding his professional sports career wasn't a total surprise.

"It's been a wild ride, that's for sure," he told Screen Slam in 2013. "2010 was my last season and in every offseason I wanted to get involved with something. And I don't know why, but I just wanted to go take an improv class.".

Industry observers note that "The improv class I wanted didn't start until January 2011, so I asked a friend who told me to go take an acting class," he recalled. "That way, at least I will be in front of people doing something while they watch. So I got into an acting class in November 2010. I loved it and stuck with it.".

Broadway emphasized that his past experience in sports stayed with him in his fresh career, especially when he worked with Gerard Butler, Aaron Eckhart and Morgan Freeman on Olympus Has Fallen.

"It was the same feeling as walking into a big-league locker room with guys that you knew were established, had earned the right to speak, and you do not have that right," he recalled. "I learned so much from these actors and everyone was so nice, but I was just watching them go about their business.”.

Industry observers note that “I did the same thing in the major leagues,” he added. “I remember the first time I was called up to Chicago, I just wanted to watch and see how these guys went about doing everything.”.

#59261. The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1326 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1326 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in May 2024, an extraordinary solar storm sent brilliant auroras across skies in parts of the world where the northern and southern lights are rarely visible.
  • The event began when a large sunspot unleashed several powerful solar eruptions in rapid succession.
  • Sources indicate that for decades, researchers have debated where the particles that make up this ring current come from.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in May 2024, an extraordinary solar storm sent brilliant auroras across skies in parts of the world where the northern and southern lights are rarely visible. But the spectacular displays were only the most obvious signs of an enormous disturbance unfolding in space around Earth. Deep within the planet's magnetosphere, the vast region controlled by its magnetic field, scientists were witnessing something they had never directly measured before.

The event began when a large sunspot unleashed several powerful solar eruptions in rapid succession. As enormous clouds of magnetized plasma raced through space, they combined before slamming into Earth's magnetosphere. The resulting storm produced the strongest magnetic disturbance ever measured in Earth's ring current, a vast region of electrically charged particles surrounding the planet.

Sources indicate that for decades, researchers have debated where the particles that make up this ring current come from. Two major sources are known: the solar wind, which carries charged particles outward from the Sun, and Earth's ionosphere, an electrically charged layer of the upper atmosphere. Both typically supply particles during geomagnetic storms, and some scientists expected the solar wind to remain an important contributor during an extreme event involving particularly dense solar wind.

Instead, the first direct measurements of ring current composition during a storm of this magnitude revealed something remarkable. Particles originating from the solar wind contributed very little, while those coming from Earth's own atmosphere dominated to an extent never previously observed.

Industry observers note that published in Science Advances, the findings suggest that Earth's atmosphere may play a much greater role in determining the severity of extreme geomagnetic storms than scientists previously recognized. Because the dominant ions from Earth are much heavier than the particles supplied by the solar wind, they may have strengthened the magnetic disturbance and caused the ring current to reach its greatest intensity unusually close to the planet.

The discovery also strengthens the case for a proposed Japanese satellite mission designed to investigate how atmospheric particles enter space and influence powerful geomagnetic storms.

How the May 2024 Solar Superstorm Disrupted Earth's Magnetic Field.

It has been revealed that on May 10 and 11, 2024, enormous clouds of charged solar particles struck Earth's magnetosphere, triggering one of the most powerful geomagnetic storms in decades. Known as the "Gannon storm" or "Mother's Day storm," the event pushed the SYM-H index, a measure of geomagnetic disturbance, to a minimum of −518 nanotesla. This represented the second-largest recorded disturbance since 1981. The previous storm of comparable strength occurred in November 2004.

Although the colorful auroras drew worldwide attention, the consequences of such storms can extend far beyond the night sky.

Recent findings suggest that "Some super or extreme geomagnetic storms are not just impressive light demonstrates -- they pose radiation risks to spacecraft, disturb GPS signals and communications, and cause power outages. Understanding how a geomagnetic storm develops is not only a scientific question, but also one with real-world consequences," said Naritoshi Kitamura, lead author and designated assistant professor from the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) at Nagoya University.

Industry observers note that A major source of these magnetic disturbances is Earth's ring current. This enormous belt of energetic charged particles, primarily oxygen and hydrogen ions, slowly circulates around the planet thousands of kilometers above the equator.

It has been revealed that as the ions move, they create an electrical current that generates its own magnetic field. That field partly opposes Earth's natural magnetic field, weakening the magnetic field measured at ground level. The resulting changes are among the key signals scientists use to track the strength of geomagnetic storms.

Japanese Satellite Reveals an Unexpected Source of Storm Particles.

In a recent development, scientists were able to investigate the May 2024 storm in unusual detail thanks to Japan's Arase satellite, which was launched in 2016 and is operated by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). The ERG (Arase) science center is jointly operated by the Institute of Space and Astronautical Science (ISAS)/JAXA and the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research/Nagoya University.

It has been revealed that arase travels through the region of space where Earth's ring current forms. Its scientific instruments can measure both the mass and energy of individual ions, allowing researchers to determine the types of particles present during a storm.

In a recent development, by remarkable timing, the spacecraft passed through the ring current shortly after the May 2024 storm began and again as the disturbance approached its peak. These observations provided a rare opportunity to examine the composition of the ring current during an exceptionally powerful geomagnetic event.

"This is the first simultaneous observation of ring current ions and solar wind during a storm this large, and the data was clear -- approximately 85% of ions were oxygen from Earth's own ionosphere," Kitamura explained.

Industry observers note that the overwhelming contribution from Earth's atmosphere was particularly surprising because the storm had been triggered by dense streams of material arriving from the Sun. Rather than supplying most of the ring current ions, the solar wind played a relatively minor role in the measured particle population.

Earth's Magnetic Field Weakened by 40%.

In a recent development, the Arase measurements revealed another extraordinary feature of the storm. The magnetic field weakened dramatically in a region much closer to Earth than where similarly severe reductions had previously been documented.

"Near the peak of the storm, Arase detected a 40% decrease in magnetic field intensity at roughly 16,000 kilometers above Earth, and much closer to Earth than similar large decreases previously documented.".

At the same time, the satellite detected a decline in the number of energetic electrons that normally circulate through this region of space.

Such an extreme weakening of the magnetic field can alter the paths followed by these electrons, causing them to drift away from their usual orbits. However, scientists have not yet determined whether the deformation of the magnetic field directly caused the observed electron loss. Further research will be needed to establish that connection.

According to recent reports, together, the observations provide new insight into how the ring current behaves during especially intense geomagnetic storms. They also suggest that the unusually large population of heavy ions originating from Earth's atmosphere may have helped produce the severe magnetic disturbance so close to the planet.

A New Clue to Predicting Dangerous Solar Storms.

It has been revealed that the findings could have vital implications for space weather forecasting. Current models rely heavily on conditions in the solar wind to estimate how powerful an approaching geomagnetic storm might become.

However, the latest measurements suggest that conditions within Earth's own upper atmosphere could also influence a storm's eventual intensity. Understanding how many atmospheric ions escape into the magnetosphere, and how they contribute to the ring current, may therefore be essential for making more reliable predictions.

Sources indicate that the researchers believe that additional satellite observations could help answer these questions. Their findings support FACTORS, a proposed mission involving two satellites that is being prepared for an upcoming JAXA proposal opportunity.

FACTORS would investigate the processes that allow ions from Earth's atmosphere to flow into the magnetosphere and examine how those particles contribute to the development of geomagnetic storms.

In a recent development, by revealing how Earth's atmosphere and incoming solar material interact during extreme events, the mission could eventually improve forecasts of dangerous space weather. More accurate predictions would help scientists better anticipate storms capable of disrupting satellites, navigation systems, communications networks, and power infrastructure.

Materials provided by Nagoya University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

American Airlines stated Wednesday it's bringing small, fresh "bites" to first class on flights between its hubs in New York and Chicago, the carrier's latest effort to win over higher-spending customers.

The changes start this month. Customers will be able to pick between two options, which include prosciutto and melon or apple cinnamon chia pudding for breakfast and a Thai noodle salad or mezze plate for lunch and dinner, American said Wednesday.

American last offered fresh food for first class on these routes in 2019, a spokeswoman said. Currently, customers in first class on these flights get a smaller, packaged snack. Airlines largely have limited food options for shorter flights, even in first class.

American has fallen behind Delta Air Lines and United Airlines in profits and investments in premium options. The airline has been working to step up those premium offerings in recent years with new cabins, lounges and aims for seatback screens on its narrow-body fleets.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after a full season of cutthroat legal proceedings, War's central divorce trial between actor Carla Duval (Sienna Miller) and tech mogul Morgan Henderson (Dominic West) has reached its final verdict. The winner? No one. But the loser? Also no one.

That's because, after some eleventh-hour heroics from mole Johnny Warren (Archie Renaux) and honeypot Flora Monroe (Rose Williams), Carla and Morgan reach their own settlement, independent of their lawyers and the judge. Following their decision, Carla will receive 50 percent of Zephyr's shares and monthly payments from Morgan until he retires. Carla and Morgan will share custody of Carla's son, Gabe (Aran Murphy). In short, it's basically what Carla had been asking for this whole time, and what the pair could have achieved without going to court.

Their decision stems from hearing Flora read Morgan's conciliatory letter to Carla, which St. John Smallwood (Pip Torrens) tried to dispose of, aloud in court. For Carla and Morgan, the letter is a reminder of the good in their relationship, something they sorely needed to recall after months of highly public mud-slinging.

"It tied itself up with humanity and kindness, and that was unexpected for me when I was reading it," Miller told Mashable in a junket interview alongside West. "I think the moral of that being that had these two people dropped their ego and their pride and nasty covetousness, if they'd let all of that go, they could have probably resolved this without the hideous experience of taking each other to court.".

"It felt like a spectacular waste of $10 million on lawyers' fees," West joked.

For series creator George Kay, there was never a version of War Season 1 where the court ruled in favor of one side or the other.

According to recent reports, "In the majority of these big divorces, the real winners are the lawyers, and so we wanted to take that agency away from the justice system and put it back in the hands of [Carla and Morgan]," Kay told Mashable in a junket interview. "So, it was always going to be down to them to work it out, which is the big expensive irony of what they've been through.".

It has been revealed that by the end of Season 1, Carla and Morgan have found what seems to be an affectionate alliance. Even though Carla now has the Zephyr shares she asked for, she won't be using them against Morgan to trigger the sale to Michael Ancker (David Menkin), as Zephyr CEO Gillian Pope (Angel Coulby) wanted. Instead, Gillian is being ousted, as it turns out she leaked the security footage of Flora leaving Morgan's hotel room to the press.

In War's final scene between Carla and Morgan, the pair stand, at peace, on a Normandy beach by their cottage.

"I'll always love you," Morgan tells Carla.

Recent findings suggest that as it seems that the pair is about to go their separate ways, Carla calls Morgan back up to the cottage for a hot chocolate with Gabe. It's proof that their life as a pairing isn't over. It's just taken a different shape. And maybe thanks to that, both Carla and Morgan "won" in the trial after all.

"The end of a divorce, it's not like someone's dead," West stated. "You either never speak to each other again, run screaming through the streets, or you realize actually why you love the person in the first place. I think that's what happens to Morgan in the end.".

"We described this divorce at the world's most expensive couples therapy, because it's only by going through everything that they've been through, hearing what the other one thinks via their lawyers, emotionally reengaging with everything they've had in their relationship, that by the end they realize what an amazing thing they have, and so we leave them okay," Kay said. "They're divorced, technically, but actually they're much better parents and they're much closer emotionally, and that was always a North Star for us.".

Sources indicate that the sweet ending for Morgan and Carla is at odds with the rest of War's bloodthirsty, win-at-any-cost tone. But for Kay, that was intentional.

In a recent development, "We didn't want it to be bleak or dark," Kay noted of the ending. "We wanted it to be redemptive.".

  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery builds on NASA's September 2025 announcement that Perseverance had identified a potential biosignature.
  • The study was co-led by Ashley Murphy, a postdoctoral researcher at the Planetary Science Institute, and Kyle Uckert, Deputy Principal Investigator of the SHERLOC instrument.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that organic carbon has been confirmed in two ancient Martian rocks examined by NASA's Perseverance rover, adding an important fresh piece to the puzzle of whether Mars once supported life. Even more surprising, the material was found just beneath the planet's surface, where harsh conditions can destroy organic compounds.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery builds on NASA's September 2025 announcement that Perseverance had identified a potential biosignature. A potential biosignature is a substance or feature that could have formed through biological activity, although other explanations are possible. Now, research published in Science Advances provides definitive confirmation that the same two rocks, located in Mars' Bright Angel formation, contain organic carbon, an essential component of life. The findings also offer a clearer picture of the material's characteristics and how it may have been preserved.

The study was co-led by Ashley Murphy, a postdoctoral researcher at the Planetary Science Institute, and Kyle Uckert, Deputy Principal Investigator of the SHERLOC instrument.

NASA's Perseverance Rover Detects Complex Organic Carbon.

Sources indicate that to investigate the rocks, researchers used the Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman & Luminescence for Organics & Chemicals (SHERLOC) instrument mounted on Perseverance's robotic arm. The instrument examined several rocks in the Bright Angel formation within Jezero crater, where the rover also collected a sample from a rock named "Cheyava Falls.".

SHERLOC uses a technique called Raman spectroscopy, which shines laser light onto a material to identify and map its minerals and organic compounds without damaging the rock.

Sources indicate that the measurements revealed macromolecular carbon (MMC), a form of carbon consisting of large, interconnected networks of carbon atoms. This type of material is also found in rocks on Earth and in meteorites. Importantly, it can form through biological activity or through chemical processes that do not involve life, so its presence alone cannot establish that Mars was once inhabited.

The surrounding geology offers additional clues about how the material reached these rocks. Billions of years ago, water flowed through a river channel into Jezero crater, carrying sediment that gradually settled on the bottom. Over time, those fine particles hardened into the mudstone formations Perseverance is now exploring.

Researchers detected the carbon within these ancient sediments and alongside carbonate and sulfate minerals that developed later as water altered the rocks. This distribution raises the possibility that organic material entered or formed within the rocks during at least two separate periods of Mars' geological history.

"While the specific formation mechanism of the MMC detected in the Bright Angel mudstones remains unknown, this is still one of the most exciting findings to date," Murphy said.

Organic Carbon Survives Just Beneath Mars' Harsh Surface.

One of the most striking results concerns where the organic carbon was found. The material survived only a few microns below the exposed Martian surface, at a depth smaller than the thickness of a sheet of paper. This is the shallowest detection of macromolecular carbon ever reported on Mars.

Sources indicate that that location makes the finding particularly unusual. Mars' surface is exposed to radiation, sunlight, and chemically reactive substances that can break down organic molecules. Scientists would generally expect these conditions to make long-term preservation especially difficult so close to the surface.

Recent findings suggest that "The Martian surface environment includes radiation and chemical oxidants that are destructive to organics, and terrestrial laboratory simulations have shown that the survival time of organics in Martian-like conditions -- especially at or near the surface -- depends on factors such as the type of organic molecule and the surrounding minerals," Murphy said. "The MMC detected in the Bright Angel mudstones is either resistant to degradation and/or has been sufficiently shielded by other minerals, such as clays, or iron-rich Martian soil.".

In other words, the carbon may have survived because of its own chemical durability, protection provided by surrounding minerals, or a combination of the two. Understanding how it endured could help scientists determine where similar organic compounds might remain preserved elsewhere on Mars.

Ancient Martian Lakes and Rivers May Have Been Rich in Organic Material.

The findings also suggest that organic carbon may not have been confined to a single region of ancient Mars.

Perseverance collected the Bright Angel sample more than 2,000 miles from Gale Crater, where NASA's Curiosity rover previously detected organic compounds. Finding organic material at such widely separated locations suggests that the chemistry associated with life's building blocks may once have been common across the Martian landscape.

Recent findings suggest that "It is encouraging for Martian habitability," Murphy said. "This indicates that billions of years ago, organics may have been more than just locally present and may have been more widely available in ancient lakes and rivers on Mars.".

According to recent reports, the possibility of widespread organic material is significant because ancient Mars once had environments containing liquid water. If organic compounds were also broadly available, some of those lakes and rivers may have offered vital chemical ingredients for life.

It has been revealed that however, discovering those ingredients does not mean that living organisms were present. Organic carbon can be produced without biology, and scientists still need to determine exactly how the material in the Bright Angel rocks formed.

Could Martian Rocks Preserve Evidence of Ancient Life?

In a recent development, determining whether the Bright Angel formation contains fossilized microorganisms remains beyond the capabilities of the rovers right now exploring Mars. Neither Curiosity in Gale Crater nor Perseverance in Jezero Crater carries the large, energy-intensive laboratory equipment needed to conclusively distinguish fossil evidence of ancient life from geological processes.

It has been revealed that perseverance was designed to search for potential biosignatures, including features like those identified in the Cheyava Falls rock. From that perspective, the discovery represents a "resounding win for Mars science," Murphy mentioned.

Sources indicate that the next major step would be to examine Martian samples using the more sophisticated instruments available in laboratories on Earth. Such equipment could reveal details too small or chemically subtle for the rover's instruments to resolve, helping researchers determine whether biological processes or nonliving chemistry produced the organic carbon.

If samples from the Bright Angel formation eventually reach Earth, scientists hope to study their minerals and organic compounds with much greater sensitivity and resolution. These investigations could help explain how the macromolecular carbon formed, how it survived, and what its presence reveals about the distribution of organic material across Mars.

In a recent development, murphy continues to collaborate with the SHERLOC science team as Perseverance explores the Martian surface. Her research also includes studying Earth materials that resemble Martian rocks and using Raman spectroscopy to improve how scientists interpret the measurements returned by the rover.

Murphy's work on SHERLOC Instrument Mars 2020 was supported through JPL Subcontract No. 1641753 to the Planetary Science Institute.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The slow international response to climate change has placed the world on a path to destruction, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told heads of state and government during opening statements at this year's COP31 climate conference.

"The ⁠brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he stated, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya to set the tone for negotiations at the UN climate summit.

Recent findings suggest that A UN reportlast month found ​the world will cross a temperature threshold countries agreed to pursue in order to prevent runaway global heating. At the same time, states like Germany are slipping down the rankings for climate action, according to the annual Climate Change Performance Index published Wednesday by Upcoming Climate Institute and Germanwatch.

Nonetheless, Guterres remarked the world has "the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach.".

Negotiators from close to 200 countries are meeting in Turkey at the end of a year characterized by extreme heat waves and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing.

At this year's talks, national representatives are discussing climate solutions such as increasing the share of electricity in an effort to move away from fossil fuels.

On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, one of the few heads of government from Europe's major economies attending the summit, said that the world's dependence on fossil fuels was at the heart of both the climate crisis and energy security challenges.

"The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security," he stated, endorsing the conference's focus on electrification which he said would lower energy bills, create jobs and protect people from the volatility of fossil fuel markets.

Burnham promised a "newly introduced era of British leadership over the next decade," announcing the UK would put climate resilience high on the agenda during its G20 presidency next year.

The US, the world's largest historical emitter of damaging greenhouse gases, is not attending the summit — for the second year in a row after US President Donald Trump withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025.

Other nations, including substantial polluters like Germany, France, Italy, Canada and Japan, also opted not to send their top leaders to the talks.

On Wednesday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who is hosting COP31 together with Australia, which is leading negotiations, called on developed nations to take greater responsibility on climate finance.

According to recent reports, financing disagreements center around who should pay for international climate action, whether funding should take the form of grants or loans and how to scale monetary support for developing nations. Many of these countries are among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis but have contributed very little to the emissions causing it.

Erdogan noted while previous conferences had resulted in different ideas around financing, they have yet to be turned into action. "We set out to make this an implementation COP," he told leaders.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addressed remarks that developed nations are not contributing enough to climate finance, saying that the transition away from fossil fuels is in "our common interest.".

Recent findings suggest that "Europe is the world's largest provider of climate finance. Last year alone, we contributed more than €32 billion [about $35.5 billion] to support developing countries," she said, adding that Europe will continue to support partners worldwide in tackling climate change.

A recent Carbon Brief analysis found that public funding pledged under the Paris Agreement to help developing countries tackle climate change fell by more than 70% in 2026.

Most multi-year pledges from donor countries expired in 2025. Since then, the US has stepped back from international climate efforts, while several European countries have cut their aid budgets, reported Carbon Brief.

Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands in the Pacific, which face an existential threat from rising sea levels, stated the response to overshoot "must be overwhelming" and promptly reversed otherwise "the world we know is over.".

"Every fraction of a degree of warming brings more catastrophe," noted Heine, adding that more warming makes it more difficult to adapt to living on a hotter planet, brings greater loss and damage from worsening weather extremes and greater financial need.

She called on leaders to triple climate finance by 2035 and make it easier for Small Island Developing States to access the money.

Sources indicate that "We are told there is no money, but their spending on war grows; the greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: Find money for life, not death. Replenish the climate funds," Heine said.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spoke of a "solemn responsibility to this and to future generations ​to act," adding that this is the critical decade.

Australia, the world's third-largest fossil fuel exporter, has vowed to promote the views of the "Pacific family" — small Pacific nations in the region such as Tuvalu or Fiji, where pre-COP meetings were held in October.

Albanese said it was crucial that climate cooperation delivered practical results — "unlocking investment in clean energy technologies, accelerating electrification, speeding up action for our oceans, unlocking climate finance for those who need it ​most.".

As reasons to speed up electrification von der Leyen pointed to wildfires in Europe and floods in Nepal, as well as droughts stretching from Central America to Sudan, and to the disruption to energy supplies linked to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

"The world is witnessing the cost of continuing with the status quo for our climate and our energy security," she mentioned, adding that the European Union would double down on efforts to become climate neutral.

"Three-quarters ​of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did ​not create and cannot ‌control," UN Secretary-General Guterres said, adding that recent conflicts have made clear a shift to renewable energy would help improve energy security and the cost-of-living crisis.

Von der Leyen also expressed support for COP31's 35-by-35 electrification pledge. The pledge aims to increase electricity's share of final global energy use to 35% by 2035, with von der Leyen saying Europe would be the first "electro-powered" continent.

Heine of the Marshall Islands noted electrification must must be strictly tied to renewable energy generation rather than fossil fuels, warning that continued oil, coal and gas extraction was a threat to her country's survival.

Recent findings suggest that iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country wanted compensation for environmental damage caused by US and Israeli strikes, including oil leaks from attacks on tankers. The strikes began in February.

Iran, which is a major fossil fuel producer and has pushed back against strict language on phasing out oil and gas at previous COPs alongside other petrostates, has also struck tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Pezeshkian linked the issue to climate finance and said his country expected "responsibility in times of war, to document and assess the environmental damages caused by military aggressions and to develop compensation mechanisms.".

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who hosted last year's COP in the Amazonian city of Belem, said the momentum for climate action had dropped off at the start of the year, partly due to the Iran war.

"We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival ‌of future generations," he said.

Sources indicate that he also warned that "climate agreements are the favorite targets of reactionary forces at COPs," and urged leaders to work together. Lula promised to protect the Amazon rainforest. "Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet," he mentioned.
